1	# Version Flow — Semantic Model
2	
3	Sources: `crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs`, `crates/callisto-graph/src/plan.rs`
4	
5	## VersionPlan
6	
7	The complete description of what needs to change. Produced by plan-generation, consumed by apply.
8	
9	Key fields:
10	- `bumps: Vec<PlannedBump>` — version changes per package
11	- `rewrites: Vec<PlannedRewrite>` — dependency spec updates in manifests
12	- `changelog_writes: Vec<ChangelogWrite>` — changelog sections to prepend
13	- `consumed_changesets: Vec<PathBuf>` — changeset files to delete after apply
14	- `pre_state_update: Option<PreState>` — pre-mode state to write to pre.json
15	- `delete_pre_json: Option<PathBuf>` — pre.json to delete (exit pre-mode)
16	
17	`VersionPlan` derives `Serialize`/`Deserialize`/`JsonSchema` but is not currently persisted.
18	This is a known gap — persisting it would enable Release Please-style resumable applies.
19	
20	## PlannedBump
21	
22	```rust
23	pub struct PlannedBump {
24	    pub package: PackageId,
25	    pub from: Version,        // expected current version before apply
26	    pub to: Version,          // target version after apply
27	    pub severity: Severity,
28	    pub governed_by: Option<GroupName>,
29	    pub reason: Option<String>,
30	    pub writes: Vec<VersionWriteTarget>,
31	}
32	```
33	
34	`from` and `to` are the idempotency anchor: the manifest's current on-disk version must equal
35	either `from` (proceed with write) or `to` (skip write, already applied).
36	
37	## VersionWriteTarget
38	
39	```rust
40	pub enum VersionWriteTarget {
41	    Manifest(PathBuf),                          // regular package manifest
42	    CargoWorkspacePackage { root_manifest: PathBuf }, // [workspace.package] version
43	}
44	```
45	
46	For `CargoWorkspacePackage`, version is read via `WorkspaceCargoResolver::workspace_version()`.
47	For `Manifest`, version is read by opening the manifest handle and reading the version field.
48	
49	## ApplyOutcome
50	
51	```rust
52	pub struct ApplyOutcome {
53	    pub lockfile_refresh_results: Option<Vec<LockfileRefreshResult>>, // always None currently
54	    pub staged: Vec<PathBuf>, // paths passed to `git add` or `git rm --cached`
55	}
56	```
57	
58	`staged` is the single source of truth for what was touched. It includes:
59	- All manifest paths (written or skipped-as-idempotent)
60	- All changeset paths (deleted or not — staged unconditionally)
61	- All changelog paths
62	- Lockfile paths (Cargo.lock, package-lock.json, etc.) for active ecosystems
63	
64	## apply_version_plan — Idempotency Guard
65	
66	### The Contract (Track B design decision)
67	
68	For each `VersionWriteTarget::Manifest(p)` in a bump's writes:
69	
70	1. Open the manifest and read the current version
71	2. If current == bump.from → call write_version, push p to modified_paths
72	3. If current == bump.to → skip write_version, still push p to modified_paths (idempotent retry)
73	4. If current is anything else → return Err(GraphError::UnexpectedManifestVersion { path: p, expected_from: bump.from, expected_to: bump.to, found: current })
74	
75	For `VersionWriteTarget::CargoWorkspacePackage { root_manifest }`:
76	Same logic, but read current version via `WorkspaceCargoResolver::workspace_version()`.
77	
78	### Changeset Staging
79	
80	Changeset paths in `plan.consumed_changesets` are ALWAYS pushed to `modified_paths`,
81	regardless of whether the file exists on disk. This enables `git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch`
82	to clean the index on idempotent retry after a crash deleted the file but didn't stage the removal.
83	
84	The current code has a bug here: it gates the push behind `if full.exists()`. Track B removes
85	this gate.
86	
87	### Why manifest path is staged even when write is skipped
88	
89	On an idempotent retry, the manifest was already written in the prior (crashed) run. The file
90	on disk is correct but may not be staged in git. Pushing it to modified_paths ensures
91	`git add` re-stages it, making the index consistent even when no bytes were changed.
92	
93	## Infrastructure Already in Place
94	
95	- `GraphError::UnexpectedManifestVersion` — error.rs, E117, fields: path, expected_from, expected_to, found
96	- `WorkspaceCargoResolver::workspace_version()` — cargo.rs, returns `Result<Option<Version>, ManifestError>`
97	- Three RED tests in apply.rs test module — see `.claude/plans/ACTIVE.md` for names
98	
99	See `.claude/specs/track-b-idempotent-apply.json` for the full testable acceptance criteria.
100

6

8	
9	| Code | Variant | When to use |
10	|---|---|---|
11	| E100 | `DuplicatePackage { id, paths }` | Same PackageId discovered at two different workspace paths |

15	| E104 | `Cycle { cycle }` | Dependency cycle detected in the workspace graph |

27	
28	| Variant | Source / Notes |
29	|---|---|
30	| `Locate(LocateError)` | Transparent from locate module |
31	| `Manifest(ManifestError)` | Transparent from callisto-manifests |
32	| `Config(ConfigError)` | Transparent; see ConfigError section below |
33	| `Format(ParseError)` | Transparent from callisto-format |
34	| `ParseChangeset { path, source }` | Changeset file parse failure (not transparent — adds path context) |
35	| `Bump(BumpError)` | Transparent from callisto-format |
36	| `Changelog(ChangelogError)` | Transparent from callisto-changelog |
37	| `Conventional(ConventionalError)` | Feature-gated; transparent |

41	| `Vcs(VcsError)` | Transparent from callisto-vcs |
42	| `Command(CommandError)` | Not transparent; wraps git/fs failures |
43	| `OnDiskVersionDrift { package, expected, found }` | On-disk version changed since plan was generated |
44	| `WorkspaceVersionConflict { root_manifest, details }` | Workspace root has conflicting version updates |
45	| `GrammarMismatch { from, to, source }` | Incompatible versioning grammars on a dependency edge |
46	
47	## ConfigError Variants
48	
49	ConfigError is always wrapped in `GraphError::Config` (transparent). All ConfigError variants
50	surface to the user as GraphError.
51	
52	### With E-codes
53	
54	| Code | Variant | When to use |
55	|---|---|---|
56	| E110 | `Read { path, message }` | Failed to read callisto.toml or moon.yml |
57	| E111 | `ParseToml { path, message }` | Invalid TOML syntax in callisto.toml |
58	| E112 | `ParseYaml { path, message }` | Invalid YAML syntax in moon.yml |
59	| E116 | `InvalidChangesetsDir { dir }` | changesets.dir escapes workspace root |
60	
61	### Without E-codes
62	
63	| Variant | Status | When to use |
64	|---|---|---|
65	| `PackageMatchedNothing { pattern }` | Defined but NEVER EMITTED — known gap | A [[package]] rule matched no packages after workspace walk |
66	| `PackageSetMatchedNothing { pattern }` | Defined but NEVER EMITTED — known gap | A [[package-set]] rule matched no packages |
67	| `OverlappingPackageSets { package, patterns }` | Defined but NEVER EMITTED — known gap | A package is claimed by two [[package-set]] rules |
68	| `ConflictingGroupNames { group, other, member }` | Active | Same member in two groups |
69	| `EmptyGroup { group }` | Active | A group has no members |
70	| `DuplicateGroupName { group }` | Active | Two groups with the same name |
71	| `UnknownRegistry { key }` | Active | publish-to references a registry key not in [registries.*] |
72	| `UnknownKey { path, key }` | Active | serde deny_unknown_fields rejection |
73	| `InvalidBumpSeverity { found }` | Active | cascade.bump-severity is not "patch" or "minor" |
74	| `InvalidPreMajorInference { found }` | Active | pre-major-inference is not a valid value |
75	| `Tag(TagTemplateError)` | Active | Invalid tag template syntax |
76	| `VersionParse(VersionParseError)` | Active | Invalid version string in config |
77	
78	## Conventions
79	
80	- Use `GraphError::Command(CommandError::Io { ... })` for filesystem I/O errors that aren't
81	  manifest parse failures.
82	- `#[diagnostic(transparent)]` variants inherit the inner type's miette diagnostic code.
83	  Do NOT add `code()` to a transparent variant.
84	- `#[allow(clippy::result_large_err)]` is set at the enum level — do not add it per-variant.
85	- New variants go at the bottom of the enum unless they belong to an existing logical group.
86	- `#[non_exhaustive]` is on both enums — external crates cannot exhaustively match them.

Draft a spec@1 for Track B: Idempotent apply_version_plan.

Write the output to `/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/specs/track-b-idempotent-apply.json`.

## Requirement

The `apply_version_plan` function in `crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs` must be made idempotent.
Currently it unconditionally calls `write_version` for every `PlannedBump`, which corrupts the
manifest if the function is re-run after a partial crash (because the manifest is already at the
target version and the write would bump it a second time).

stakeholder: release automation system / `callisto apply` command users
why: A failed `callisto apply` run must be safely retryable without manual intervention.

## Exact done_when criteria (all must be testable from outside the implementation)

1. When `VersionWriteTarget::Manifest(p)` is encountered and the manifest at `p` currently has
   version == `bump.to`, `write_version` is NOT called and no error is returned. The path `p`
   is still pushed to `modified_paths` (so `git add` re-stages it on retry).

2. When the manifest currently has version == `bump.from`, `write_version` IS called (normal
   path — not changed).

3. When the manifest currently has a version that is neither `bump.from` nor `bump.to`,
   `apply_version_plan` returns `Err(GraphError::UnexpectedManifestVersion { path, expected_from,
   expected_to, found })` and the manifest is not modified.

4. The same three-way check applies to `VersionWriteTarget::CargoWorkspacePackage { root_manifest }`,
   using `WorkspaceCargoResolver::workspace_version()` to read the current version.

5. Changeset paths in `plan.consumed_changesets` are pushed to `modified_paths` unconditionally
   — regardless of whether the file exists on disk. (This fixes a bug where `if full.exists()`
   gated the push.)

6. The three RED tests already written in `apply.rs` all pass:
   - `apply_is_idempotent_when_manifest_already_at_target_version`
   - `apply_returns_error_when_manifest_has_unexpected_version`
   - `apply_stages_changeset_path_even_when_file_already_deleted`

## out_of_scope

- `VersionWriteTarget::CargoWorkspacePackage` idempotency requires reading the workspace
  version, but there are no existing RED tests for that path — it is excluded from the
  acceptance criteria scope for this spec (criteria 4 is optional context, not a test gate).
- Lockfile refresh logic
- Rewrite and changelog write loops
- `pre_state_update` and `delete_pre_json` handling
- Persisting `VersionPlan` to disk

## Infrastructure already in place (do NOT re-add these)

- `GraphError::UnexpectedManifestVersion` — `crates/callisto-graph/src/error.rs`, E117,
  fields: `path: PathBuf`, `expected_from: Version`, `expected_to: Version`, `found: Version`
- `WorkspaceCargoResolver::workspace_version()` — `crates/callisto-manifests/src/cargo.rs`

## Implementation site

`crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs`, lines 75-93 (the `for bump in &plan.bumps` block).
Replace the unconditional `handle.write_version(...)` call with the three-way version check.

Also line ~132: remove the `if full.exists()` gate before `modified_paths.push(cs_path.clone())`.

## Spec format

Output a spec@1 JSON object conforming to the standard. Save it to:
`/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/specs/track-b-idempotent-apply.json`

id should be SPEC-001.

---
name: feedback-canon-pipeline-scope
description: Canon auditor loop smell — when spec starts describing implementation prose, stop iterating
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

The canon pipeline (drafter → auditor → exit-gate) is the right process. But when the auditor's "fix" suggestions start prescribing exact control flow, method names, or error propagation paths, that is a signal to stop the audit loop — not to keep refining.

**Why:** At that point the spec is just the implementation rewritten in English. Further audit rounds add noise, not precision. Three rounds should be the limit; if the spec still fails after three clean rewrites, the remaining issues are probably auditor over-reach, not real spec gaps.

**How to apply:** After two audit rounds, read the remaining issues critically. If they're asking "which method is called" or "which ? arm fires first" — those belong in implementation notes or api_surface, not in acceptance criteria. Accept the spec and move on. If they're asking "what observable behavior does the caller see" — those are real gaps worth fixing.

**Never:** Let the auditor push so many "untestable" flags that the criteria list becomes a prose description of the implementation.

49	impl PackagePattern {

51	    pub fn matches(&self, id: &PackageId) -> bool  // checks id.name() only, not ecosystem
52	    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str
53	}
54	```
55	
56	`matches()` tests `id.name()` against the glob pattern. It is intentionally ecosystem-agnostic:
57	`[[package-set]] match = "foo-*"` applies to `cargo:foo-bar`, `npm:foo-bar`, etc. all at once.

60	
61	For each discovered package, `ManifestWalkResolver::build` resolves an override in two steps:
62	
63	### Step 1: [[package]] rule lookup
64	
65	Current code (first-match-wins, declaration order):
66	```rust
67	let pkg_override = cfg.packages.iter()
68	    .find(|(pattern, _)| pattern.matches(&id))

70	```

73	```
74	Collect all matching [[package]] rules.
75	If any are Prefixed-pattern matches → use the first Prefixed match.
76	If none are Prefixed → use the first Bare match.
77	If no matches → None.
78	```

92	```

96	1. `[[package]]` with Prefixed PackageId pattern (e.g. `match = "cargo:foo"`)
97	2. `[[package]]` with Bare PackageId pattern (e.g. `match = "foo"`)
98	3. `[[package-set]]` with matching glob (e.g. `match = "foo-*"`)

# Vector Planning Skill

<overview>
Vector decomposes a spec@1 into a sequenced, bite-sized plan@1 that a developer or agent can execute without making any design decisions. Every task is independently testable, time-bounded, and fully specified down to exact code and commit messages.
</overview>

---

<sub_skills>

### vector/plan
Invoke vector-planner to decompose a spec@1 into an ordered sequence of implementation tasks. Each task includes exact file paths, a failing test, minimal implementation, expected test output, and a commit message.

### vector/estimate
Invoke vector-estimator to assign effort estimates (in minutes) to each task in a plan@1, identify parallelizable tasks, and surface blocking dependencies.

### vector/challenge
Invoke vector-challenger to adversarially review a plan@1 for missing tasks, wrong ordering, under-specified steps, over-sized tasks, and missing error handling.

### vector/decompose
Decompose a large or ambiguous task into smaller, dependency-ordered sub-tasks before planning. Use when a single task in the plan would exceed 15 minutes or require the implementer to make a design choice.

</sub_skills>

---

<artifact_contracts>

**Consumes**: `spec@1`
**Produces**: `plan@1`

<tdd_requirement>

Every task in a plan@1 follows this exact sequence:

1. Write the failing test
2. Run the test — confirm it fails with the expected error
3. Write the minimal implementation to make the test pass
4. Run the test — confirm it passes
5. Commit with the conventional commit message

A task that starts with implementation before a failing test violates this requirement.

</tdd_requirement>

<no_placeholders_rule>

Every step must show exact code. "Implement the feature", "add appropriate error handling", and "write tests as needed" are not steps — they are abdications. If the exact code is not known, it must be derived from the spec and documented as a concrete choice, not deferred as a TBD.

## Critical facts the previous plan got wrong — read these carefully

**Packages map keys are ALWAYS Bare, never Prefixed.** `ignore_walk.rs` builds ids via `PackageId::parse(name).unwrap_or_else(|_| PackageId::Bare(name))` from the raw manifest name. `key.ecosystem()` is always None. Do NOT write code that calls `key.ecosystem()`.

**Ecosystem for AC-5 comes from `pkg.manifests`, not from the map key.** For each entry (key, pkg) where `pattern.matches(key)` is true, iterate `pkg.manifests`, filter to `d.role == ManifestRole::Canonical`, and collect `d.ecosystem()` (returns `Ecosystem` directly — not `Option<Ecosystem>`, no unwrap needed). Collect into a `BTreeSet<Ecosystem>`.

**The only real trigger for the cross-ecosystem diagnostic is the napi case.** A package with both Cargo.toml and package.json in the same directory (same workspace path) maps to a SINGLE packages entry with TWO canonical ManifestDecls. Two packages with the same name in DIFFERENT directories is a `DuplicatePackage` error that returns before the diagnostic pass.

**Test fixture for AC-5:** Create a temp dir with a single subdirectory containing both `Cargo.toml` and `package.json`, each declaring `name = "my-pkg"`. Construct a fake `ResolvedConfig` with `packages = vec![(PackageId::Bare("my-pkg".into()), some_config)]`. The workspace walk of that temp dir will produce one `Package` entry with two canonical manifests (CargoToml + PackageJson), and the bare rule will match it. The distinct-ecosystem set will be `{Cargo, Npm}` → diagnostic fires.

**Do NOT create fixtures with two directories containing the same package name** — that triggers DuplicatePackage, not the diagnostic.

## Correct implementation for Fix 2 (AC-5 diagnostic pass)

After `packages.insert(id, pkg)` loop (around walk.rs line 201), add:

```rust
// Cross-ecosystem diagnostic: warn when a bare [[package]] rule matches a
// package whose manifests span multiple ecosystems.
use std::collections::BTreeSet;
for (pattern, _) in &cfg.packages {
    if pattern.ecosystem().is_some() {
        continue; // Prefixed rules never trigger this diagnostic
    }
    let ecosystems: BTreeSet<Ecosystem> = packages
        .iter()
        .filter(|(key, _)| pattern.matches(key))
        .flat_map(|(_, pkg)| {
            pkg.manifests.iter()
                .filter(|d| d.role == ManifestRole::Canonical)
                .map(|d| d.ecosystem())
        })
        .collect();
    if ecosystems.len() >= 2 {
        let eco_list: Vec<&str> = ecosystems.iter().map(|e| e.prefix()).collect();
        diagnostics.push(Diagnostic {
            code: DiagnosticCode::BareRuleMatchesMultipleEcosystems,
            severity: DiagnosticSeverity::Warning,
            message: format!(
                "[[package]] rule `{}` matches packages in multiple ecosystems ({}); \
                 use an ecosystem-prefixed pattern like `{}/{}` to target only one",
                pattern.name(),
                eco_list.join(", "),
                ecosystems.iter().next().map(|e| e.prefix()).unwrap_or("cargo"),
                pattern.name()
            ),
            package: None,
            path: None,
            escalated_by: None,
            governed_by: None,
        });
    }
}
```

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

## What Track E was really about at the semantic model level

At the identity resolution layer, Callisto's packages-map is ecosystem-agnostic by construction — all keys are `PackageId::Bare`. Config rules (`[[package]]`) live in a different namespace that allows Prefixed patterns. Track E's actual problem was that there's an **impedance mismatch between two identity spaces**: the rule-authoring space (where humans think in ecosystems) and the resolution space (where packages are flat names). The specificity ordering we added is one mechanism for navigating that mismatch — but it's a partial one.

The spec was written too narrowly because it addressed *symptoms* (the wrong rule wins) rather than the *semantic operation* (what does it mean to resolve config for a package?).

---

## What the spec should have defined

**A canonical resolution operation, not a patch to a lookup.**

There is no function `resolve_package_config(id, cfg) -> PackageConfig` in the codebase. Instead, the lookup lives inline at every call site. Walk.rs and aggregate.rs are two of those sites. There may be others. The spec should have:

1. **Inventoried all lookup sites** as a non-negotiable first step — treating "any call to `cfg.packages.iter().find(...)`" as a lookup site, not just the one in scope.
2. **Defined a single extraction**: one function, one place, one test suite.
3. **Made every call site a migration task**, with a red test that proves the old call site produces wrong behavior and the new call site produces right behavior.

Instead we patched walk.rs in scope and discovered aggregate.rs post-exit-gate as a sibling gap. That's not a reviewer catch — it's a spec design failure. The spec didn't model the operation; it modeled a file.

## The ordering invariant is unspecced

The spec says "first Prefixed match wins" (AC-3) without defining what *first* means. In the implementation, it means BTreeMap/Vec iteration order on `cfg.packages`. That could be:
- TOML declaration order (if the collection is insertion-ordered)
- Sorted key order (if it's a `BTreeMap`)

The test AC-3 uses `cargo/multi` vs `npm/multi`, where BTreeMap sorted order and TOML declaration order coincide (`cargo < npm` alphabetically). So AC-3 passes regardless of which semantic is actually implemented. The spec should have explicitly stated: **"Within each tier, resolution is stable TOML declaration order"**, and the test should have been written to distinguish the two orderings — e.g., `npm/foo` declared first, `cargo/foo` second, asserting `npm/foo` wins. As written, we can't tell from the test suite which ordering the implementation actually delivers.

## Prefixed-pattern semantics are syntactic, not semantic — and the spec doesn't say so

When `npm/cross-eco` matches a Cargo-only package, the prefixed rule wins. This is the AC-1b behavior. But the spec never explicitly names the design decision: **"A prefixed pattern wins by virtue of its syntactic form, not by whether the package has manifests in that ecosystem."**

That's a real design choice with real UX implications. A user who writes `npm/my-crate` to configure only the npm face of a dual-ecosystem package will silently apply that config to a Cargo-only package named `my-crate`. There's no warning. The cross-ecosystem diagnostic covers the inverse case (bare rule matching multi-ecosystem packages) but not this case (prefixed rule with ecosystem mismatch).

The full diagnostic surface — what conditions SHOULD produce a warning — was never specced. AC-5 covers one case. The complementary case goes uncovered, not because someone decided it was out of scope, but because the spec framing never asked the question.

**Layer 1 — The resolution model** (what the operation IS)

- State the ordering invariant explicitly: TOML declaration order, preserved through config loading.
- State that Prefixed patterns match by name; ecosystem prefix signals specificity tier only.

**Layer 2 — The implementation contract** (how it must be built)

git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fix(graph): idempotent apply_version_plan; add lockfile refresh on apply

apply_version_plan now reads the on-disk manifest version before writing:
if it already equals the plan's target, the write is skipped (safe to
retry after a crash) but the path is still staged for git; if it matches
neither the plan's from nor to version, returns the new
GraphError::UnexpectedManifestVersion (E117) instead of silently
clobbering an unexpected workspace state. Also fixes a changeset-staging
bug where a deleted changeset's path was only pushed to modified_paths
inside the exists() branch, leaving it out of git's staging on retry
after a prior partial run had already deleted the file.

Also adds ApplyOptions.refresh_lockfiles: when set, runs `cargo update
--workspace` / `uv lock` / `poetry lock --no-update` for ecosystems with
active bumps before the staging pass, recording results in
ApplyOutcome.lockfile_refresh_results. Prevents `cargo publish --locked`
failing with a stale lockfile after a version bump.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01NSixbn1hHH7WLXGqzF3GCz
EOF
)"

content.text: Clean. Committing the squashed publish-pipeline hardening commit.

input.command:
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
feat(publish): package filter, registry resolution, subprocess hardening

Squashes several tightly cross-referential publish-pipeline changes that
would not build standalone if split further:

- plan_publish/publish gain a --package filter (errors on unknown names
  rather than emitting an empty plan) and convert previously-fatal git/
  changeset/tag lookup failures into soft Diagnostics.
- npm publishConfig.access/registry is now read from package.json and
  respected over the scoped-package --access public default; fixes
  publishing to a private registry with publishConfig.access: "restricted".
- SubprocessRegistryClient (publish_client.rs) now runs each publisher
  from the package's own directory instead of the workspace root, guards
  against publishing a version that doesn't match the plan, runs
  `python -m build` before `twine upload` (twine had no dist/ artifacts
  on a clean checkout), adds npm --registry / pnpm --no-git-checks / bun
  lockfile support, fixes PEP 427 wheel-filename normalization (dots
  weren't collapsed, only hyphens), fixes a false-positive rate-limit
  match on cargo's "429.1KiB compressed" summary line, and extends
  already-published detection to npm/twine E409 and mixed skip+upload
  output.
- Publish orchestration caps rate-limit retries (MAX_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES)
  so a 429 loop can no longer hang forever, adds a progress callback so
  `callisto publish` prints per-package status, and treats is_published()
  errors as non-fatal (falls through to attempt publish rather than
  aborting on a flaky pre-check).
- CommandRunner gains run_with_timeout (default delegates to run(), so
  existing mock runners are unaffected); CliCommandRunner implements it
  with spawn+poll+kill and background-thread stderr streaming to avoid
  pipe deadlock. Used for the 300s publish subprocess timeout.
  New CommandError::TimedOut (E025).
- PublishAttemptResult::Failed now carries a machine-readable `kind`
  (serialized as errorKind: rateLimited/authFailed/network/other) derived
  from RegistryError::kind_str(), so callers can distinguish failure
  types without parsing the message string. Wired through the text
  renderer and JSON report output.
- RegistryKey gains PYPI/NUGET well-known constants, consumed by
  PublishTarget::{Pypi,NuGet}::registry_key().

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01NSixbn1hHH7WLXGqzF3GCz
EOF
)"

20	| `napi.targets` | napi-rs (Node.js native) | Array of Rust target triples |
21	| `[tool.maturin].targets` | maturin (Python native) | Array of Rust target triples |
22	| `engines.node` | npm | Range string only; no discrete version expansion |
23	| `requires-python` | PyPI | PEP 440 range string |
24	| `<TargetFramework>` / `<TargetFrameworks>` | .NET | MSBuild TFM strings |
25	| `<RuntimeIdentifiers>` | .NET AOT | RID strings for native AOT publish |
26	
27	Java (Maven/Gradle) and C# runtime versions are in scope for the `RuntimeVersionEntry` type
28	model (see §2) but their manifest readers are Phase 4 (Java) and Phase 5 (C# runtime
29	versions) work. This document marks them as **planned** at each relevant point.
30	
31	### 1.1 Non-goals
32	
33	See §8 for the complete enumerated list. Summary: no YAML generation, no manylinux compat-tag
34	inference, no external HTTP calls.
35	
36	### 1.2 Relationship to §G.8.4
37	
38	The existing `napi.rs` module (§G.8.4 of `docs/01-spec.md`) provides `triple_to_role` and
39	`role_to_triple` — the canonical, fixtured table mapping Rust target triples to
40	`ManifestRole::Platform` values. The matrix subcommand extends that table's scope from
41	drift-checking to report emission. The table itself is not duplicated; `callisto-graph`'s
42	`napi.rs` is the single source of truth.
43	
44	---
45	
46	## 2. JSON output contract — `MatrixReport`
47	
48	The report is emitted as a single JSON object. All package names are the registered package
49	name (the `name` field in `package.json`, `[package] name` in `Cargo.toml`, or
50	`<PackageId>` in a `.csproj`).
51	
52	```jsonc
53	{
54	  "platformTargets": {
55	    "<package_name>": { /* PlatformTargetGroup */ }
56	  },
57	  "runtimeVersions": {
58	    "<package_name>": { /* RuntimeVersionEntry */ }
59	  }
60	}
61	```
62	
63	A workspace with no napi, maturin, or runtime-version constraints produces:
64	
65	```json
66	{ "platformTargets": {}, "runtimeVersions": {} }
67	```
68	
69	This is a valid, non-error output (exit 0).
70	
71	### 2.1 `PlatformTargetGroup`
72	
73	```jsonc
74	{
75	  "kind":    "napi" | "maturin" | "dotnet-aot",
76	  "source":  "<manifest field name>",  // "napi.targets", "[tool.maturin].targets", "<RuntimeIdentifiers>"
77	  "targets": [ /* Vec<PlatformTarget> */ ]
78	}
79	```
80	
81	`source` is the raw field name as it appears in the manifest, for auditability. It is not a
82	path — the manifest path is implicit in the package.
83	
84	### 2.2 `PlatformTarget`
85	
86	```jsonc
87	{
88	  // Exactly one of these two identity fields is present, never both:
89	  "triple":  "<rust-target-triple>",   // napi and maturin only
90	  "rid":     "<dotnet-rid>",           // dotnet-aot only
91	
92	  "platform":      "darwin" | "linux" | "win32" | "freebsd" | "android" | "wasi" | "unknown",
93	  "arch":          "arm64" | "x64" | "ia32" | "arm" | "riscv64" | "ppc64" | "s390x" | "wasm32",
94	  "abi":           "gnu" | "musl" | "gnueabihf" | "musleabihf" | "msvc" | null,
95	  // abi is null for: darwin, freebsd, android, wasi, and win32 (msvc is implicit on win32
96	  // and is omitted from the JSON value rather than emitted as "msvc").
97	
98	  "hostRunner":    "macos-latest" | "macos-13" | "ubuntu-latest" | "windows-latest",
99	  "useCross":      true | false,
100	  "artifactName":  "native-<triple>" | "native-<rid>",
101	  "packageDir":    "<workspace-root-relative path>",
102	  "packageName":   "<registered package name>"
103	}
104	```
105	
106	`packageDir` is the directory that must contain the native artifact before `callisto publish`
107	runs. For napi packages it is the path from the platform manifest entry; for maturin and
108	dotnet-aot it is the package root.
109	
110	`hostRunner` is the cheapest GitHub Actions runner that can build the target. Targets that
111	require cross-compilation always set `useCross: true`; they still run on `ubuntu-latest`
112	unless the toolchain requires otherwise. See §3 for the complete per-triple table.
113	
114	### 2.3 `RuntimeVersionEntry`
115	
116	```jsonc
117	{
118	  "ecosystem":        "npm" | "python" | "java" | "dotnet",
119	  "field":            "<manifest field name>",
120	  "range":            "<raw field value>",
121	  "targetFrameworks": ["<tfm>", ...]  // dotnet multi-targeting only; null or absent otherwise
122	}
123	```
124	
125	`range` is always the raw string from the manifest. No normalization, no expansion to discrete
126	versions. Callers that need discrete version lists must expand the range themselves using
127	ecosystem-appropriate tooling.
128	
129	`targetFrameworks` is present and non-null only when the .NET project uses
130	`<TargetFrameworks>` (plural) rather than `<TargetFramework>`. It contains the split list of
131	TFM strings. A `<TargetFramework>` (singular) project produces `"range": "net9.0"` with
132	`"targetFrameworks": null`.
133	
134	Java (`ecosystem: "java"`) and dotnet runtime versions (`ecosystem: "dotnet"`) are **planned**
135	for Phase 4/5 respectively. The type is defined now to keep the contract stable; the readers
136	are not yet implemented.
137	
138	---
139	
140	## 3. The napi-rs target triple table
141	
142	All 18 targets supported by napi-rs as of 2026. This table is the authoritative mapping used
143	by both the drift cross-check (§G.8.4) and the matrix report emitter. Maintenance point:
144	`crates/callisto-graph/src/napi.rs`, function `triple_to_role`.
145	
146	### 3.1 napi-rs / maturin Rust triple table
147	
148	| Rust triple | platform | arch | abi | hostRunner | useCross |
149	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
150	| `aarch64-apple-darwin` | darwin | arm64 | — | macos-latest | false |
151	| `x86_64-apple-darwin` | darwin | x64 | — | macos-13 | false |
152	| `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` | win32 | x64 | — | windows-latest | false |
153	| `i686-pc-windows-msvc` | win32 | ia32 | — | windows-latest | false |
154	| `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` | win32 | arm64 | — | windows-latest | false |
155	| `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` | linux | x64 | gnu | ubuntu-latest | false |
156	| `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` | linux | x64 | musl | ubuntu-latest | true |
157	| `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` | linux | arm64 | gnu | ubuntu-latest | true |
158	| `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` | linux | arm64 | musl | ubuntu-latest | true |
159	| `armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf` | linux | arm | gnueabihf | ubuntu-latest | true |
160	| `armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf` | linux | arm | musleabihf | ubuntu-latest | true |
161	| `riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu` | linux | riscv64 | gnu | ubuntu-latest | true |
162	| `powerpc64le-unknown-linux-gnu` | linux | ppc64 | gnu | ubuntu-latest | true |
163	| `s390x-unknown-linux-gnu` | linux | s390x | gnu | ubuntu-latest | true |
164	| `aarch64-linux-android` | android | arm64 | — | ubuntu-latest | true |
165	| `armv7-linux-androideabi` | android | arm | — | ubuntu-latest | true |
166	| `wasm32-wasi` | wasi | wasm32 | — | ubuntu-latest | false |
167	| `x86_64-unknown-freebsd` | freebsd | x64 | — | ubuntu-latest | true |
168	
169	Notes:
170	- `osx-x64` (macOS Intel) maps to `macos-13`, which is the last GitHub-hosted runner with an
171	  Intel CPU. `macos-latest` is M1+ (arm64) only as of 2024.
172	- `win32` targets never carry `abi` in the JSON output; msvc is the only Windows ABI napi-rs
173	  supports and emitting it would be redundant.
174	- Darwin and freebsd targets carry no ABI field; `android` and `wasi` targets carry no ABI
175	  field.
176	- An unrecognised triple produces a warning diagnostic named `UnknownNapiTriple` and is
177	  excluded from `targets[]`. It never causes a hard error.
178	
179	### 3.2 .NET RID table
180	
181	| .NET RID | platform | arch | abi | hostRunner | useCross |
182	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
183	| `win-x64` | win32 | x64 | — | windows-latest | false |
184	| `win-arm64` | win32 | arm64 | — | windows-latest | false |
185	| `linux-x64` | linux | x64 | gnu | ubuntu-latest | false |
186	| `linux-arm64` | linux | arm64 | gnu | ubuntu-latest | true |
187	| `linux-musl-x64` | linux | x64 | musl | ubuntu-latest | true |
188	| `linux-musl-arm64` | linux | arm64 | musl | ubuntu-latest | true |
189	| `osx-x64` | darwin | x64 | — | macos-13 | false |
190	| `osx-arm64` | darwin | arm64 | — | macos-latest | false |
191	
192	These are the eight RIDs supported for native AOT cross-platform publishing. Additional RIDs
193	declared in `<RuntimeIdentifiers>` that are not in this table produce an
194	`UnknownDotnetRid` warning diagnostic and are excluded from `targets[]`.
195	
196	---
197	
198	## 4. Artifact naming convention
199	
200	```
201	napi/maturin:  artifactName = "native-{triple}"
202	               example: "native-aarch64-apple-darwin"
203	
204	dotnet-aot:    artifactName = "native-{rid}"
205	               example: "native-linux-arm64"
206	```
207	
208	This naming is the contract between the build phase and the publish phase:
209	
210	- **Build phase**: `callisto-build-action` (§7) uploads an artifact under this name after a
211	  successful compilation. The artifact contains exactly one binary file at the artifact root:
212	  a `.node` file (napi), a wheel `.so`/`.dylib`/`.dll` (maturin), or a self-contained
213	  executable (dotnet-aot).
214	- **Publish phase**: the orchestrating action (§6) downloads each artifact by `artifactName`
215	  and places the binary into `packageDir` before `callisto publish` runs. `callisto publish`
216	  then finds the binary in the expected location and includes it in the registry upload.
217	
218	The naming scheme is chosen to be unique within a single workflow run (no two entries in
219	`platformTargets` share a `triple` or `rid`) and stable across runs (so artifact caching
220	strategies based on the name are safe).
221	
222	---
223	
224	## 5. `callisto matrix` CLI surface
225	
226	```
227	callisto matrix [--package <name>] [--format json|table]
228	```
229	
230	### 5.1 Flags
231	
232	| Flag | Default | Description |
233	|---|---|---|
234	| `--package <name>` | all packages | Restrict output to a single package by registered name |
235	| `--format json\|table` | `json` | Output format. `table` renders a human-readable ASCII table |
236	
237	### 5.2 Exit codes
238	
239	| Code | Condition |
240	|---|---|
241	| 0 | Success, including the case where the report is empty (no napi/maturin/runtime targets found) |
242	| 1 | A manifest read error occurred (file unreadable, malformed TOML/JSON/XML) |
243	
244	An empty report is not an error. A workspace that has no napi packages, no maturin packages,
245	and no `engines.node` / `requires-python` constraints exits 0 with `{"platformTargets":{},"runtimeVersions":{}}`.
246	
247	### 5.3 Output ordering
248	
249	Keys in both top-level maps are sorted lexicographically by package name. `targets[]` entries
250	within a `PlatformTargetGroup` are sorted by triple/RID string, so the output is
251	deterministic and diff-friendly.
252	
253	### 5.4 `--format table`
254	
255	The table format is for human inspection only. Its schema is not part of the stable contract.
256	CI pipelines must use `--format json`.
257	
258	---
259	
260	## 6. GitHub Actions integration contract
261	
262	The matrix feature has two touchpoints in the GitHub Actions workflow.
263	
264	### 6.1 `nativeMatrix` output — the strategy matrix source
265	
266	The orchestrating step (the `callisto-orchestrate` step in `callisto-action`) runs
267	`callisto matrix --format json` early in the publish branch (after confirming no pending
268	changesets) and emits the `targets[]` array as an action output named `nativeMatrix`.
269	
270	```yaml
271	# In the orchestrate step, publish branch:
272	MATRIX_JSON=$(callisto matrix --format json | jq '[.platformTargets[].targets[]] | unique_by(.artifactName)')
273	echo "nativeMatrix=$MATRIX_JSON" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
274	```
275	
276	Consumer workflows pipe this into a downstream build job:
277	
278	```yaml
279	jobs:
280	  matrix:
281	    outputs:
282	      nativeMatrix: ${{ steps.callisto-orchestrate.outputs.nativeMatrix }}
283	
284	  build-native:
285	    needs: [matrix]
286	    if: ${{ needs.matrix.outputs.nativeMatrix != '[]' }}
287	    strategy:
288	      matrix:
289	        target: ${{ fromJson(needs.matrix.outputs.nativeMatrix) }}
290	    uses: ./.github/actions/callisto-build-action
291	    with:
292	      target: ${{ toJson(matrix.target) }}
293	```
294	
295	### 6.2 Artifact routing — placement before publish
296	
297	Before `callisto publish` runs, the orchestrating step downloads each artifact by
298	`artifactName` and places it into `packageDir`.
299	
300	Contract for artifact content: the downloaded artifact must contain exactly one binary at the
301	artifact root. The binary is:
302	
303	- A `.node` file for napi (the output of `napi build`).
304	- A Python wheel `.whl` file for maturin.
305	- A self-contained executable (no extension on Linux/macOS, `.exe` on Windows) for dotnet-aot.
306	
307	The placement step is:
308	
309	```yaml
310	- name: Download native artifacts
311	  run: |
312	    MATRIX_JSON='${{ needs.matrix.outputs.nativeMatrix }}'
313	    echo "$MATRIX_JSON" | jq -c '.[]' | while read -r target; do
314	      ARTIFACT=$(echo "$target" | jq -r '.artifactName')
315	      DIR=$(echo "$target" | jq -r '.packageDir')
316	      gh run download --name "$ARTIFACT" --dir "$DIR"
317	    done
318	```
319	
320	---
321	
322	## 7. `callisto-build-action` composite action design
323	
324	Location: `.github/actions/callisto-build-action/action.yml`
325	
326	### 7.1 Inputs
327	
328	| Input | Required | Description |
329	|---|---|---|
330	| `target` | yes | JSON string of one `PlatformTarget` object (§2.2) |
331	
332	### 7.2 Dispatch on `kind`
333	
334	The action reads `target.kind` to select the build toolchain:
335	
336	#### kind = `napi`
337	
338	```yaml
339	- uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
340	  with:
341	    targets: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).triple }}
342	
343	- name: Install cross (if needed)
344	  if: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).useCross }}
345	  run: cargo install cross --git https://github.com/cross-rs/cross
346	
347	- name: Install napi-rs CLI
348	  run: npm install -g @napi-rs/cli
349	
350	- name: Build native module
351	  run: |
352	    TARGET='${{ fromJson(inputs.target).triple }}'
353	    CROSS='${{ fromJson(inputs.target).useCross }}'
354	    PKG_DIR='${{ fromJson(inputs.target).packageDir }}'
355	    cd "$PKG_DIR"
356	    if [[ "$CROSS" == "true" ]]; then
357	      napi build --platform --release --target "$TARGET" --cross-compile
358	    else
359	      napi build --platform --release --target "$TARGET"
360	    fi
361	
362	- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
363	  with:
364	    name: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).artifactName }}
365	    path: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).packageDir }}/*.node
366	```
367	
368	#### kind = `maturin`
369	
370	```yaml
371	- uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
372	  with:
373	    targets: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).triple }}
374	
375	- uses: PyO3/maturin-action@v1
376	  with:
377	    target: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).triple }}
378	    args: --release --out dist
379	    manylinux: auto
380	
381	- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
382	  with:
383	    name: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).artifactName }}
384	    path: dist/
385	```
386	
387	#### kind = `dotnet-aot`
388	
389	```yaml
390	- uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
391	
392	- name: Publish native AOT
393	  run: |
394	    RID='${{ fromJson(inputs.target).rid }}'
395	    PKG_DIR='${{ fromJson(inputs.target).packageDir }}'
396	    cd "$PKG_DIR"
397	    dotnet publish -r "$RID" -c Release -o out/
398	
399	- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
400	  with:
401	    name: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).artifactName }}
402	    path: ${{ fromJson(inputs.target).packageDir }}/out/
403	```
404	
405	### 7.3 Runner selection
406	
407	The action is dispatched from a matrix whose `runs-on` is set to `target.hostRunner`. The
408	action itself does not override the runner; that is the matrix job's responsibility.
409	
410	---
411	
412	## 8. Non-goals
413	
414	The following are explicitly out of scope for the matrix feature, now and in future phases
415	unless a separate spec extends this one:
416	
417	1. **YAML generation for GitHub Actions workflows.** `callisto matrix` emits JSON data; the
418	   calling workflow is responsible for its own structure.
419	
420	2. **Inferring maturin targets from manylinux compat tags.** The mapping from
421	   `manylinux_2_17_x86_64` to a set of Rust triples requires external configuration that
422	   maturin itself does not embed in `pyproject.toml`. The matrix reader requires explicit
423	   `[tool.maturin] targets = [...]`.
424	
425	3. **Fetching current LTS version lists from external services.** `engines.node` and
426	   `requires-python` are emitted as raw range strings. Converting `>=20` to `[20, 22, 24]`
427	   requires an HTTP call to the Node.js release schedule or PyPI classifiers; that is outside
428	   callisto's hermetic-by-design scope (§13 invariant, no `reqwest`/`octocrab` dependency).
429	
430	4. **Java JNI platform matrix.** The JVM is inherently portable; JNI native libraries are
431	   rare enough in monorepo contexts that the cross-product of JVM versions times native
432	   targets is not worth a generalized model. Java appears in `RuntimeVersionEntry` only (Maven
433	   `<java.version>`, Gradle `sourceCompatibility`), and that reader is Phase 4 work.
434	
435	5. **Matrix subcommand for Go.** Go's cross-compilation story (`GOOS`/`GOARCH` env vars) does
436	   not follow a manifest-declared target list pattern, and Go does not produce language-native
437	   binary modules in the napi/maturin/dotnet-aot sense.
438

content.text:
The spec lives at `.claude/specs/callisto-matrix.md` — status `PLANNED (Phase 3 / v0.5)`. It's a real design doc, not yet run through the canon→vector→lambda pipeline as a formal `spec@1`. It's fairly thorough already: JSON output contract (`MatrixReport` → `platformTargets`/`runtimeVersions`), CLI surface (`callisto matrix [--package] [--format json|table]`), the napi-rs 18-triple table (reused, not duplicated, from `napi.rs`), a .NET RID table, and a full GitHub Actions integration design including a new `callisto-build-action` composite action.

I checked what's actually there to implement it against:

**Already done:** the napi-rs triple table (`napi.rs`, committed this session as `12dcde2`) — the spec explicitly says this is the single source of truth to reuse, not duplicate. That's the one piece for free.

**Missing, and non-trivial:**
- The `callisto matrix` CLI subcommand itself — doesn't exist at all.
- `MatrixReport`/`PlatformTargetGroup`/`PlatformTarget`/`RuntimeVersionEntry` model types — none exist.
- A maturin reader (`[tool.maturin].targets` in `pyproject.toml`) — `python.rs` exists but doesn't read this field.
- `engines.node` (npm) and `requires-python` (PyPI) range extraction — neither is currently parsed anywhere; would need small new readers.
- **A .NET/csproj manifest reader from scratch.** Callisto has zero .NET support today — no XML parsing, no `csproj` reader, nothing. `Ecosystem::NuGet` exists as an enum variant but nothing implements it. This is the biggest chunk: `<TargetFramework(s)>` and `<RuntimeIdentifiers>` reading means building an entire new ecosystem module.
- The `callisto-build-action` composite action (napi/maturin/dotnet-aot build dispatch) — new file, doesn't exist.
- Wiring the CI `nativeMatrix` output (already stubbed in `ed074a4`) to call the real subcommand instead of falling back to `{}`.

This is bigger than Track B/E/F combined — mainly because of the .NET piece, which is a genuine new-ecosystem build, not a wire-up. The spec's own phasing already treats Java and C# *runtime versions* as later phases (4/5); .NET *platform targets* (RIDs) are nominally in this phase but are separable the same way.

questions.question: The matrix spec covers three target kinds: napi (Node.js native), maturin (Python native), and dotnet-aot (.NET native, requires building a whole new csproj/.NET manifest reader from scratch). How should we scope the first pass?

options.label: napi + maturin first (Recommended)
options.description: Reuses existing manifest infrastructure (npm.rs, python.rs). Ship the CLI subcommand, JSON contract, and GH Actions integration for these two now; defer dotnet-aot to a follow-up spec once there's a reason to build .NET support.

options.label: Full spec including .NET
options.description: Build the csproj/.NET manifest reader as part of this pass too. Bigger scope, but delivers the complete Phase 3 spec in one go.

questions.question: This is a substantial new feature (new CLI command, new model types, new manifest readers). Should it go through the same canon→vector→lambda spec/plan/implement pipeline used for Track B/E/F, or move faster with direct implementation?

options.label: canon→vector→lambda pipeline (Recommended)
options.description: Formal spec@1 + adversarial audit/exit-gate, then a TDD plan, then implementation with red/green phases and review after each task. Matches how the rest of this session's work was done — slower but produces the same verification rigor.

options.label: Direct implementation
options.description: I implement against the existing markdown spec directly, writing tests as I go, without the formal spec@1/plan@1 ceremony. Faster, less adversarial verification.
